sentences.text: Garudimimus was an ornithomimosaur, a group of dinosaurs known for their bird-like features, that possessed a unique mix of ancient and advanced anatomical traits.
The single known individual measured nearly 3.5 meters in length and weighed between 77.3 and 98 kilograms.
Unlike earlier members of its family, this dinosaur had toothless upper and lower jaws.
Its body plan included relatively short, stocky hindlimbs, robust feet, and reduced ilia, the hip bones that connect the spine to the pelvis.
The genus was formally described by Rinchen Barsbold in 1981.
The only known specimen, the holotype — the specific specimen the species is based on — was discovered in 1981 by a Soviet-Mongolian expedition at Bayshin Tsav.
This skeleton is currently catalogued as MPC-D 100/13.
It likely fed on plants or small animals, using a horny beak to compensate for its reduced bite force.
The structure of its pelvic girdle and hindlimbs suggests it had poor running abilities.
Evidence points to the animal having shaggy feathering, similar to that seen in large, flightless modern birds like ratites.
Analysis of its eye rings indicates it was active during both day and night, functioning as a cathemeral herbivore.
There is only one known species, Garudimimus brevipes.
When first described in 1981, Barsbold placed it in its own family, Garudimimidae.
Modern studies often group it within the family Deinocheiridae as the sister taxon to Deinocheirus.
This dinosaur lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous period.
Its fossils were found in the Bayan Shireh Formation at the Bayshin Tsav locality, which dates from approximately 95.9 ± 6.0 to 89.6 ± 4.0 million years ago.
It was once thought to have a lacrimal horn, but later redescription revealed this was actually a distorted prefrontal bone.
Early interpretations suggested the foot had an arctometatarsalian condition, a specific arrangement of metatarsal bones.
Some researchers also claimed it possessed a nasal horn similar to that of Pelecanimimus.
However, a 2005 redescription by Kobayashi and Barsbold refuted many of these previous anatomical interpretations.
The placement of Garudimimus within the Deinocheiridae remains disputed among scientists.
